chunks.text: The Mast Tree, commonly sold and grown as Polyalthia longifolia, belongs to the custard-apple family Annonaceae; recent botanical revision has moved the species into the genus Monoon as Monoon longifolium, though the older name Polyalthia longifolia remains in wide everyday use. It is native to southern India and Sri Lanka but is now planted throughout the tropics, from Jakarta to Trinidad and Tobago, prized for its neat, symmetrical, pyramidal shape. The tree grows to over 20 metres with willowy, weeping, pendulous branches and long, narrow, lance-shaped leaves with wavy (undulate) margins; new leaves emerge coppery-brown, pass through a light green stage, and mature to dark green. Spring brings small, star-shaped, pale green flowers that last two to three weeks, followed by clusters of 10–20 fruits that ripen from green to purple or black.

It is grown almost entirely as an ornamental and screening tree — its dense, columnar form makes it a popular choice as a living privacy screen and windbreak/noise barrier along roads in India — and it can be clipped into various shapes as a garden focal point. Its flexible, straight, lightweight trunk was historically used to make masts for sailing ships, which is the origin of the English name 'Mast Tree'; the timber is also used today for small articles such as pencils, boxes and matchsticks. Seed oil from the tree has shown antioxidant, anti-lipoxygenase and antimicrobial activity in laboratory studies, and methanolic extracts of the plant have yielded numerous organic compounds, some with cytotoxic properties, though these findings are research-stage rather than established medicine. Ecologically, its leaves are a larval food plant for the tailed jay and common/lime butterflies, and its fruit is eaten by Asian koels and flying foxes.

Despite the common name 'False Ashoka', this species is botanically unrelated to the true, sacred Ashoka tree (Saraca asoca) of Indian religious tradition, and the two are frequently confused in everyday usage. Its leaves are also used decoratively as festoons during festivals in parts of India.
